newsitem.title: THAILAND: Morgan Stanley sees U.S. correction help Asia.
newsitem.headline: Morgan Stanley sees U.S. correction help Asia.

text.p: A sharp correction of U.S. stock markets by mid-1997 would likely help revive interest in underperforming Asian bourses, said Morgan Stanley's chief global strategist Barton Biggs.
Biggs picked South Korea, India and Thailand as potential beneficiaries of a 10-30 percent correction of the Dow Jones Industrial Index this year.

Biggs told an investment seminar that he saw signs of a slowdown in capital flows into U.S. equities and forecast a sharp decline in the Dow Jones Industrial Average this year as more investors switch funds out of U.S. markets.

"There will be shifting among mutual funds, and aggressive U.S. investors will shift from technology and aggressive growth funds to international funds because they are looking for action. I believe that in that environment, they will change to Asian funds and emerging growth markets," Biggs said.
"Asian markets could rise 15 percent and if things work out in Thailand, India and Korea, then those markets could be up 30-35 percent in 1997," he said.
"We really are focused on the Asian markets that are down and are depressed and where people are bearish" he added.

On Thailand which has been hit by fears attributed to slowing economic growth and a high current account deficit, Biggs dismissed concerns about a banking crisis and described the current level of the Thai baht as "about right".
The investment strategist said he was "concerned and cautious" on U.S. equities this year, seeing their correction as historically overdue.
"Earnings growth (from equities) four times as fast as the economic growth simply isn't sustainable," Biggs said.
Forecasting two percent U.S. economic growth for 1997 and continued low inflation, Biggs said a simple slowdown in positive news could spark a correction in the U.S.
"At the top of a bull market, the news doesn't have to be bad. It just has to be less good," Biggs said.
Biggs said the dollar is now peaking and the yen is set to strengthen sharply this year. He saw three percent Japanese economic growth in 1997.

Biggs, chairman of Morgan Stanley Asset Management Inc, said his firm reduced its exposure to general equities in the last three weeks to 56 percent of its total portfolio investment from 74 percent earlier.
He said three percent of the trimmed exposure was switched to U.S. treasury bills, and the remaining 15 percent was kept in cash.
